item.title: More steps in place to meet the goal of common prosperity
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
A decade-old liquor and tobacco shop near where I stay in Beijing shut down last year for unknown reasons. When it reopened recently, the glowing neon signboard outside announced that it was now a "heartwarming station" for people who work in the open air, such as street cleaners, delivery riders and taxi drivers. Inside the 150-square-meter station there are some sofa sets, five or six tables with chairs, a water heater, a microwave oven, mobile phone chargers and a first-aid kit. Outside, there is a toilet and several charging piles for e-bikes. Such stations, as I learned from a volunteer, are designed to provide free service to street cleaners, delivery riders, taxi drivers and whoever needs help. Since they are air-conditioned, those working long hours in the open can relax on the sofas, have a cup of tea, enjoy some snacks and have their phones and bikes recharged before returning to work. According to a recent report, Beijing now has 1,364 such stations operated by subdistricts, neighborhood committees and delivery platforms whose employees benefit from such units. Many other cities in China also have similar government-supported projects. Before these stations came up, some banks in Beijing were letting workers who slog it out in the open come in to escape the cold, heat, wind or rain. The establishment of such heartwarming stations is only one of many measures the central authorities and local governments have taken to help disadvantaged groups. Most cities in China offer free bus rides to senior citizens in their territory. That is why, on boarding a bus in China, one sees that most passengers are senior citizens. While many retired people are joining square dancing or chorus singing activities, some others are engaging themselves in city tours by taking advantage of the free bus ride policies. The fact that Beijing alone has 1,252 bus routes covering a total length of 28,928 kilometers should keep senior citizens busy for a couple of years. Senior citizens also enjoy free entry or discounted tickets to most of the museums, parks, scenic spots and tourist attractions. While others have to register beforehand and pay to get into popular tourist attractions, senior citizens mostly have to just show their ID card to get in without any appointment. At many places, senior citizens are also entitled to free annual physical checkups and vaccines. When I entered a community clinic in Sanya, Hainan province, last year looking for a massage, the doctor told me they don't provide such services but could arrange for someone to give me a massage on the condition that I agree to a free physical checkup at the clinic. It sounded odd to me, but I guess the local medical authorities must have set a goal for each community clinic to provide free medical checkups to a certain number of senior citizens. In many cities, local governments are offering people above a certain age (80 in Beijing) subsidized renovation of their washrooms to make the facilities senior citizen-friendly. Senior citizens living alone at home are visited several times a day by volunteers and neighborhood committee members to make sure they are fine. In rural areas, most farmers, unlike their urban counterparts, did not contribute to any social insurance during their working ages, but those aged above 60 are now entitled to a retirement pension ranging from the national minimum of 163 yuan ($24.46) to as high as 1,555 yuan ($233.3) in Shanghai, depending on financial conditions in different localities. The rural pensions largely come from government subsidies. Humble as the sum is at the moment, millions of elderly farmers have welcomed it as a good and right measure, as otherwise they would have had to be financially dependent on their children in their old age. Building sidewalks for those who are visually impaired is becoming a normal practice in city planning and renovation while more and more buses are now equipped with wheelchair lifts to make movement more convenient for people who use wheelchairs. Numerous employment fairs are organized each year by local governments to help the country's more than 10 million university graduates get jobs. Free vocational training is provided to teach new skills to those who are unemployed, thus increasing their employability. With 2026 coming to an end, the central authorities are holding meetings to bring in greater measures to help disadvantaged groups and to make sure that no one is left behind in the country's pursuit of common prosperity. I pray it is a success. The author is former deputy editor-in-chief of China Daily. kangbing@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China launches 6G innovation pilot across eight provinces and municipalities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
China's top industry regulator launched a ministry-province collaborative pilot program for 6G innovation and development in Shanghai on Tuesday, with Beijing, Hebei, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Hubei, and Guangdong approved to carry out 6G pilot work. The launch marks a key step in China's push to advance 6G development from technology research to coordinated regional experimentation, laying the groundwork for the country's participation in global 6G standardization and industrial deployment. The pilot program, initiated by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, focuses on utilizing local conditions within the national-level framework. Key tasks include strengthening research on 6G-related industries such as new-type terminals, key chips and components, instruments, and satellite internet, as well as on potential 6G application scenarios including immersive communications, industrial manufacturing, the low-altitude economy, and the marine economy. The initiative aims to form a nationally coordinated development pattern for 6G. Research on 6G technical standards has also entered a sprint phase, according to the IMT-2030 (6G) Promotion Group, China's top-level coordination platform for 6G research and development. Under the timeline set by international standards organizations, the first version of 6G international standards is expected to be released in the first half of 2029, while basic research on 6G standards is scheduled to be completed in the first half of 2027.

item.title: Cook Islands scientist joins historic deep-sea dive
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
A scientist from the Cook Islands has become the first person from her country to directly observe the deep-sea seabed within its exclusive economic zone, joining a dive aboard China's manned submersible Jiaolong in the Manihiki fracture zone on Nov 21 local time, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Tuesday. Chloe Wragg joined Chinese scientists Yang Yifan and Zhao Shengya aboard the submersible to conduct an environmental survey. The mission successfully achieved its objectives, collecting valuable deep-sea environmental data and samples. The successful dive highlights the blue partnership between China and the Cook Islands and further strengthens their cooperation in deep-sea science and technology, the ministry said. Following the dive, Wragg expressed her excitement at witnessing the milestone firsthand. She said the Cook Islands has long been at the forefront of deep-sea scientific research and that the dive demonstrated the country's determination and commitment to deepening its understanding of its own seabed. She also expressed her gratitude for the opportunity to work with colleagues from the National Deep Sea Center and the Second Institute of Oceanography, both under the Ministry of Natural Resources. Wragg said the expedition reflected the longstanding friendship and scientific ties between the two countries, as well as their close relations and extensive exchanges. The expedition marks the second joint marine scientific mission between China and the Cook Islands, following their first such mission in 2025. During the current expedition, Jiaolong is scheduled to conduct five dives in the Cook Islands' exclusive economic zone. The mission aims to help the country fill gaps in its basic deep-sea data and train its first group of local researchers in crewed submersible operations through hands-on experience.

item.title: Chronicles bring history back to life
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
In the early 20th century, geologist Ding Wenjiang made a field visit to what is now Yunnan province to survey local mineral resources. To gain a basic understanding of the region's historical heritage, he consulted a Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) chronicle of Yunnan, which quoted passages from another book that introduced metallurgy with exceptional clarity and detail. Ding managed to track down the original book, titled The Exploitation of the Works of Nature, a centuries-old Chinese scientific classic known as Tiangong Kaiwu, and later facilitated its reprint. Since then, the long-forgotten masterpiece that systematically documents the agriculture and handicraft technologies of ancient China has gradually become known to contemporary Chinese. Zhang Zhiqing, former executive deputy director of the National Library of China, said that local chronicles played a big role in the rediscovery of the book, adding that the story was precisely a microcosm of how local chronicles — reference books that comprehensively and systematically document the history and current state of the natural environment, politics, economy, culture and society of a given administrative region — preserve details of local history. President Xi Jinping's consistent attention to local chronicles has greatly boosted their development, bringing continuous progress across China, Zhang noted. In the 1980s, when Xi worked in Zhengding county of Hebei province and later in Fujian province, he paid close attention to local records. Attracted by Zhengding's profound cultural heritage, he read the county's chronicles and other historical records thoroughly, surveyed historical sites and immersed himself in the county's culture, building a deep and comprehensive understanding of Zhengding. In 1989, at a meeting in Ningde, Fujian, Xi noted that the first thing he did upon arrival was to read the local prefecture's and county's chronicles. He said that to grasp a region's defining features, one must first understand its history, and studying local chronicles offers a reliable way to do so. A county's history is best recorded in its county's chronicle, while a prefecture's chronicle is even more comprehensive, recording positive as well as negative figures, Xi said. Chronicles can tell us what happened there, and we can learn from them, he added. In 2006, when he inspected Cangnan county, Zhejiang province, to check the post-disaster recovery efforts following Super Typhoon Saomai, Xi, then secretary of the Communist Party of China Zhejiang Provincial Committee, consulted the county's chronicles and, in a meeting with local officials, read aloud historical records of typhoons that had struck the area. He urged the officials to learn from history, make science-based decisions and improve their ability to respond to typhoons and other natural disasters. In 2014, during a visit to the Capital Museum in Beijing, Xi, who became general secretary of the CPC Central Committee in 2012, called for officials to attach equal importance to exhibition and the compilation of history in order to inspire national pride and confidence. During the 23rd group study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee in 2020, Xi urged efforts to bring back to life relics collected in museums, legacies on the vast land of China and records in ancient books. Zhang Yi, deputy head of the local literature group of the Library of Ancient Books of the National Library of China, said Xi's instructions have given a strong boost to the development of local chronicles. A number of documents have been formulated to guide the development of local chronicles. "Consolidating and improving local chronicles" was included in the outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) issued in March. Zhang Zhiqing, former National Library of China executive deputy director, said that local chronicles have a long history in China and developed into a form of local encyclopedia during the Southern Song Dynasty (1127-1279). Since then, the tradition of compiling local chronicles every 30 to 50 years under the central government's order took shape, with all regions following the same style. With the emergence of local chronicles, ancient China's historical records came to comprise three tiers: The state had its national history; each region had its local chronicles; and each family had its genealogy, he said. "Local chronicles are a literature form unique to China. Other countries certainly have local historical records as well, but compiling them regularly and continuously under the central government's order and in the same style is rarely seen elsewhere. This stems from China's pluralistic yet unified political landscape," he added. Historical insight A major function of local chronicles is to support political governance. "Historically, many local systems and customs did not emerge uniformly or remain unchanged. Policies took shape differently across regions and evolved over time, often being adapted, modified or supplemented to fit local realities. Politicians therefore need to understand how these policies evolved step by step before they can design policies that are realistic, effective and feasible, and turn historical experience into a useful reference for present-day governance," said Zhang Yi, from the Library of Ancient Books. Moreover, details of history that can hardly be found in official history books can be traced in chronicles. For example, ancient Chinese had the habit of erecting stone tablets to commemorate notable figures. Many of them have disappeared over the long course of history, but much of their content has been recorded in chronicles and passed down. President Xi has also stressed the importance of compiling local chronicles. At a meeting in Ningde in 1989, he said that compiling chronicles is a meaningful task, and that its significance, in plain terms, lies in helping us become people who see things clearly. According to Liu Yongqiang, deputy director of the China Local Chronicles Work Office, since the beginning of reform and opening-up in 1978, two rounds of national efforts to compile local chronicles took place in China, with the latest round concluding in 2020. During the two rounds, more than 10,000 provincial, city and county level chronicles were compiled, and nearly 4,000 old chronicles were collated. The two rounds "systematically documented the history and current conditions of regions across the country, promoting cultural prosperity and laying a solid foundation for cultural construction, social development and the passing down of the national spirit", said Liu, who added that the third round is about to begin. Xue Changlin, a member of the Sichuan Local Records Association, said that at a time of deepening reform and opening-up, profound social transformation and the wave of digital change, the third round, compared with the previous two, will be a more challenging task. "It's not a simple continuation or comprehensive revision, but a systematic cultural project that will adapt to the development of the new era, reconstruct the local chronicle system and reflect the new face of the times," Xue said.

item.title: Firsthand lessons essential in Sino-US relations
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
During his visit to the United States in September, Chinese President Xi Jinping invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study over the next five years. A similar invitation given in 2023 saw 50,000 young Americans visit China over the following three years. The 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong province, underscored the importance of cooperation in an increasingly divided world. But lasting cooperation requires more than agreements among governments; it also depends on people who can understand different societies and communicate across cultural differences. Educational exchanges, particularly among young people, can help build the mutual understanding and trust needed for this cooperation. While a large number of Chinese students have gone to the US, relatively fewer Americans have studied in China. According to the Institute of International Education, 1,749 US students studied in China for academic credit in 2023-24, compared with 277,398 Chinese students enrolled in US institutions that year. Although these figures are not directly comparable, they illustrate the imbalance in educational exchange between the two countries. That landscape is gradually changing. Chinese universities have made substantial advances in research capacity and international engagement. The 2025 Nature Index ranked Zhejiang University, Tsinghua University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University third, fourth and fifth, respectively, in its overall institutional table. China ranked first among countries and territories. While these rankings measure research output in selected scientific journals rather than the overall quality of universities, they demonstrate China's growing research strength. China is also attracting students from around the world. Official data show that during the 2024-25 academic year, about 380,000 international students from 191 countries and regions studied or participated in exchange programs in China. To revitalize the educational relationship between China and the US, we must look beyond university campuses. Both high school students and university students can benefit from visiting China. Stepping outside one's comfort zone, engaging with unfamiliar ideas and reconsidering familiar assumptions can help students become more independent and critical thinkers. Studying abroad provides a richer basis for forming their own judgments. There is also a distinctive educational value in being a minority. Students studying in a society where their language, cultural references and everyday habits are not the norm must learn to listen carefully, communicate across differences and see themselves through other people's eyes. They may experience the discomfort of not immediately understanding how things work, but that discomfort can be productive, fostering humility, adaptability and a greater appreciation of diverse perspectives. These experiences can have lasting professional value. China is the world's second-largest economy and a key player in global manufacturing, trade, technology and scientific research. For US graduates entering international business, technology, academia, journalism or public service, firsthand experience of China can be a differentiating asset in the job market. Employers working across borders may value candidates who understand not only China's economic importance but also its business practices, consumers, institutions and social context. A person who has studied in China brings something different from someone whose knowledge comes solely from coursework, news coverage or occasional business meetings. I first visited China in 1981. Since then, I have returned many times, including periods of living and working here and engaging with Chinese universities, businesses and policymakers. The China I saw on my first visit bears little resemblance to today's China. This has reinforced one belief: countries are difficult to understand when viewed only from afar. The US has benefited greatly from generations of Chinese students who studied at US universities and contributed to research, business and communities there. China has likewise benefited from Chinese students who studied abroad and returned with knowledge, networks and new perspectives. A larger flow of US students to China would not diminish the appeal of US universities. Nor should US students be expected to return with uniform views of China. But what matters is that their judgments are informed by firsthand experience rather than only from a distance. The benefit of bringing 100,000 young Americans to China should not be measured simply by the number of visitors. Its greater value lies in creating opportunities for young Americans and Chinese to learn from one another and develop more nuanced perspectives. A more balanced educational exchange can create something both countries need: more people capable of understanding the other side without necessarily agreeing with it. That is a worthwhile investment, not only in education, but also in the future of China-US relations. The author is executive vice-chancellor, American president, and distinguished professor of social science at Duke Kunshan University in China. The views do not necessarily reflect those of China Daily. item.title: Opening-up, tech strength fuel APEC
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
As the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies navigate a changing global landscape, China's continued opening-up and strengths in advanced manufacturing and green technologies are creating massive new opportunities for businesses across the Asia-Pacific region, executives of multinational corporations said. These strategic developments are becoming increasingly crucial for enhancing regional productivity. By combining China's rapid technological innovation and immense market scale with the complementary resources of other APEC economies, businesses are moving beyond transactional relationships toward deeper partnerships to build a resilient and sustainable future for the region, they said. For multinational companies, turning these shared opportunities into practical outcomes requires combining global operational experience with China's manufacturing ecosystems. Mark Kouwenhoven, general manager of China operations at Australian metal mining and energy company Fortescue, noted that a major opportunity lies in connecting China's strengths with practical industrial needs across the Asia-Pacific. Fortescue is actively working with Chinese partners on battery-electric mining equipment and integrated green grids to decarbonize its operations in Australia's Pilbara region. This strategy was echoed by BHP, an Australian multinational mining and metals corporation, which sees vast potential in deepening its two-decade-long cooperation with China beyond traditional commodity trade. Catherine Raw, chief development officer of BHP, highlighted the company's partnership with leading Chinese steelmakers to develop lower-emissions blast furnaces and carbon capture solutions. China brings a strong problem-solving mindset and the ability to scale solutions quickly, which, combined with BHP's resources, creates real potential to solve shared decarbonization challenges, she said. This accelerating cross-border integration is already evident in macroeconomic metrics. China's trade in high-tech products with other APEC economies surged 50.3 percent year-on-year to reach 6.66 trillion yuan ($997.34 billion) in the first three quarters, exceeding the total for the whole of last year. The country's imports of electronic components from other APEC economies increased 56 percent during the same period, according to data from the General Administration of Customs. Henry Liu, vice-president for Asia-Pacific operations at Lubrizol, a global provider of specialty chemicals in the United States, said China's comprehensive industry infrastructure serves an exceptional range of applications where customer needs are first tested and validated. As other APEC economies industrialize, matching products and supply chains refined in China with local requirements can significantly shorten the time taken to reach the market, he said. Liu emphasized that China's "AI plus" initiative and proven green technologies allow neighboring economies to adopt established, commercially competitive solutions. This enables a faster, more economic development path with lower investment requirements and faster deployment at scale. This surge in technological exchange is also transforming the region's aviation and logistics infrastructure. Cathay Group, a travel lifestyle brand based in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, is leveraging the mainland's artificial intelligence advancements by deploying over 120 AI models to optimize aircraft scheduling, personalize customer experiences and manage complex cargo requirements. Arnold Cheng, Cathay Group director for the Chinese mainland, said that AI-assisted screening is proving particularly vital for Cathay in identifying shipments that may require additional import or export license checks. To advance the green transition, Cathay fully supports the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area's competitive sustainable aviation fuel value chain, which is vital for the aviation sector to reach net-zero emissions, he said. Similarly, ContiTech, one of the world's leading industrial specialists for material solutions, is applying its advanced materials expertise to support expanding AI infrastructure across the region. The company is developing highly efficient liquid cooling systems for data centers, meeting the growing infrastructure demands of the digital economy. Concurrently, ContiTech is expanding its localized industrial portfolio and developing high-pressure hydrogen refueling solutions in China to serve the broader Asia-Pacific market. Ultimately, capitalizing on these diverse trends requires a commitment to local adaptation. zhengxin@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Pakistani astronaut preparing for the Shenzhou XXIV mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
"I was the last one to join the program. But now I can confidently say that from that last one to becoming the first one to be in space." Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is preparing for the Shenzhou XXIV mission after completing a year-long training program in just seven months. Starting from scratch, he learned Chinese and can now read through the entire mission checklist. For Ali, learning Chinese is more than mastering a language — it's a way to connect with the Chinese people and understand their hearts.

item.description:

David Taupiac, secretary of the French National Assembly and member of the National Assembly for Gers, said in an interview with China Daily that China-France cooperation is flourishing across a wide range of fields and holds tremendous potential, from shared favorites such as wine and duck to cutting-edge industries including the French aeronautical sector and China's electric vehicle and robotics industries. Watch the video to learn more!

item.title: Pakistani astronaut set to become first foreign crew member aboard Tiangong
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24
China's Tiangong space station is poised to welcome its first foreign astronaut — Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who will also become the first citizen of his country to travel beyond Earth's atmosphere. The wing commander in the Pakistan Air Force is set to fly to the orbital outpost with two Chinese astronauts — Major General Tang Hongbo, commander of the Shenzhou XXIV mission, and Colonel Wu Yi, the crew's spaceflight engineer. Their spacecraft is scheduled to lift off aboard a Long March 2F rocket at 8:18 am on Wednesday from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, Zhang Jingbo, a senior engineer and spokesman for the China Manned Space Agency, said. At a news conference on Tuesday morning at the Jiuquan spaceport, Zhang told reporters that the rocket's propellant injection was scheduled to begin at its service tower later that day and that other prelaunch preparations were proceeding in an orderly manner. "After the Shenzhou XXIV spacecraft enters its preset orbital position, it will activate the rapid autonomous rendezvous-docking mode and use about three and a half hours to approach and connect with the front port on the Tianhe core module," he said.

item.title: NVIDIA board reinstates Jensen Huang
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
SAN FRANCISCO -- US chipmaker NVIDIA announced Monday that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the company's president and chief executive officer (CEO), as well as a member of its board of directors, with immediate effect. In a statement, Nvidia said its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with him. The board said it was satisfied with Huang's candor and ability to lead the company. The board also said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and, based on that input, was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," said Harvey C. Jones, chair of the board. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company," he said. "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said, cited by the statement. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 amid mounting pressure over his extramarital affairs. Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress was appointed as interim CEO. Under the latest decision, Kress will continue to serve as CFO, while Jones will remain board chairman. "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," US President Donald Trump said on Monday following NVIDIA's announcement.
